skill.name: pytm
skill.description: Create Python-based threat models with pytm, including STRIDE analysis, trust boundaries, data flows, diagrams, and threat reports.
skill.summary: Build threat models as code with pytm and STRIDE.
skill.author: AgentSecOps

security_audit.summary: The audit found extensive Markdown examples and inline code that static analysis misclassified as shell backtick execution. Two sudo package installation examples are confirmed because they require elevated privileges, while the hardcoded URLs are documentation references.

remediation.issue: Privileged package installation appears in setup examples.
remediation.suggestion: Tell users to review and approve graphviz installation before running sudo commands, and provide non-privileged alternatives where possible.

remediation.issue: The skill references helper scripts and resources that are not present in the scanned file tree.
remediation.suggestion: Bundle the referenced scripts and templates or revise the instructions so users do not attempt to run missing local files.

content.value_statement: Threat modeling can be hard to keep current when architecture changes quickly. This skill helps Claude, Codex, and Claude Code create pytm models, review STRIDE threats, and document mitigations.
actual_capabilities: Explains how to define pytm trust boundaries, actors, servers, datastores, and data flows.
Guides STRIDE review for spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, and privilege escalation.
Shows CI examples for running threat model checks and storing generated diagram artifacts.
Provides patterns for web applications, microservices, custom threats, and trust boundary analysis.
Suggests ways to document mitigations, residual risk, and security review outputs.
limitations: It is documentation-focused and does not include the referenced helper scripts in the scanned package.
It depends on users installing pytm and graphviz before diagrams can be generated.
Generated threats still require human validation against the real system design.
It may expose sensitive architecture details if reports are shared too broadly.

use_cases.title: Create an application threat model
use_cases.description: Define system components, trust boundaries, and data flows as a pytm model for a new product design.

use_cases.title: Add threat modeling to CI
use_cases.description: Run a threat model script in pull requests and publish diagrams or unmitigated threat checks as build artifacts.

use_cases.title: Review architecture changes
use_cases.description: Compare updated data flows against STRIDE categories and document new mitigations before release.

prompt_templates.title: Start a basic model
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for a small web application.
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me create a simple pytm threat model for a web app with a user, web server, API server, and database. Include trust boundaries and encrypted data flows.

prompt_templates.title: Review STRIDE coverage
prompt_templates.scenario: Validate an existing model for missing security attributes.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my pytm component list and data flows for STRIDE coverage. Identify missing authentication, authorization, encryption, logging, or trust boundary details.

prompt_templates.title: Plan CI integration
prompt_templates.scenario: Add repeatable checks to a development workflow.
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a CI workflow that runs my pytm model, generates a diagram, and fails when high-risk threats do not have documented mitigations.

prompt_templates.title: Create custom threats
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me define custom pytm threats for cloud storage, API abuse, and weak service-to-service authentication. Include conditions, mitigations, and review guidance.

output_examples.input: A team asks for a threat model for a three-tier web application.
output_examples.output: A structured model outline with internet, DMZ, and internal trust boundaries, key data flows, STRIDE review points, and mitigation tasks.

output_examples.input: A security engineer wants to check if a new API gateway changes risk.
output_examples.output: A focused review of authentication, authorization, rate limiting, logging, and cross-boundary flows affected by the gateway.

output_examples.input: A DevSecOps engineer wants threat modeling in pull requests.
output_examples.output: A CI plan that installs required tooling, runs the model, stores diagram artifacts, and reports missing mitigations.

best_practices: Keep model files close to architecture changes so reviews stay current.
Use placeholders for secrets and sensitive architecture details in shared reports.
Review generated STRIDE threats with engineers who understand the actual system.
anti_patterns: Do not treat generated threats as a complete security review without human validation.
Do not publish diagrams that reveal sensitive network or trust boundary details.
Do not run privileged installation commands without confirming the package source and need.

faq.question: What does this skill help me build?
faq.answer: It helps build pytm threat models with components, data flows, trust boundaries, STRIDE threats, and mitigations.

faq.question: Does it run pytm automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides guidance and examples. Users must install dependencies and run commands in their own environment.

faq.question: Can it replace a security architecture review?
faq.answer: No. It supports review preparation, but generated threats need human validation and business context.

faq.question: Why does it mention graphviz?
faq.answer: pytm can use graphviz to generate data flow diagrams from the model.

faq.question: Can I use it in CI/CD?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill describes CI patterns for running a threat model and checking mitigation completeness.

faq.question: What should I avoid putting in a model?
faq.answer: Avoid real secrets, private network details, and sensitive architecture information unless access is controlled.
